questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish conventional interest from compensatory interest, as explained in the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales. Which of the two do the Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules govern?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Conventional interest is the compensation a borrower pays for the use of money in an onerous loan; it is agreed upon by the parties and must be expressly stipulated in writing. Compensatory interest (also called penalty interest, indemnity or moratory interest) is the indemnity for damages arising from the debtor's delay in an obligation to pay a sum of money; it is allowed by law even without a promise to pay interest, and the parties may stipulate it through a penal clause. The Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules govern only compensatory interest.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts v. Midtown, the Court held that conventional interest "is therefore paid not as a consequence of default, nor is it compensatory or a result of a provision of law"; it is the result of the express will of the parties and is allowed only if there is an express stipulation in writing. Compensatory interest "is the indemnity for damages arising from delay on the part of the debtor in an obligation consisting in the payment of a sum of money," allowed by law in the absence of a promise to pay interest. The Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules "govern only compensatory interest, not conventional interest," read with Articles 2209 and 1226.
suggestedAnswer.application: So a borrower not in delay owes only the principal and conventional interest; if the borrower is in delay, compensatory interest accrues as a matter of law in addition to conventional interest.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Conventional = agreed price of money, in writing; compensatory = indemnity for delay, by law or penal clause. **Bar trap:** do not apply the Eastern Shipping/Nacar legal rates to replace the parties' conventional interest.

keyPoints: Conventional interest: price for the use of money; express stipulation in writing required
Compensatory interest: indemnity for delay in paying a sum of money; allowed by law
Compensatory interest may be stipulated through a penal clause
Debtor in delay: compensatory interest accrues in addition to conventional interest
Eastern Shipping and Nacar govern only compensatory interest

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part I (the two kinds of interest)
source.excerpt: Conventional interest is therefore paid not as a consequence of default, nor is it compensatory or a result of a provision of law. It is "rigorously lucrative," and the result of the express will of the parties in a contract. … Compensatory interest, also referred to as penalty interest, indemnity, or moratory interest, is the indemnity for damages arising from delay on the part of the debtor in an obligation consisting in the payment of a sum of money. It is interest allowed by law in the absence of a promise to pay interest as compensation for delay in paying a fixed sum or a delay in assessing and paying damages. … It should be stressed that the Eastern Shipping Lines and Nacar rules govern only compensatory interest, not conventional interest, and should be read in conjunction with the provisions of Articles 2209 and 1226 of the Civil Code.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In 2025, L lent ₱500,000 to B at a stipulated interest of 3% a month (36% a year). B defaults and, when sued, argues that the rate is unconscionable. L argues that since usury ceilings were lifted, the parties are free to agree on any rate. How should the court approach the question, and what happens if the rate is struck down? Explain, citing the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The lifting of the interest ceilings does not give lenders a free hand: a stipulated rate that is unconscionable may be equitably reduced. Since 36% is more than twice the prevailing legal rate (6%), it is suspect, and L must prove that the rate is required by prevailing market conditions and that the parties were on equal footing. If the rate is struck down, only the rate is nullified; the agreement to pay interest remains, and the legal rate prevailing when the agreement was made applies.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts v. Midtown, the Court held that stipulated rates are subject to the unconscionability standard, determined by the context of each case. "The legal rate of interest is the presumptive reasonable compensation for borrowed money ... in cases where stipulated interest is more than twice the prevailing legal rate of interest, it is for the creditor to prove that this rate is required by prevailing market conditions"; the creditor must also show the parties were on an equal footing. Where the monetary interest rate is found unconscionable, "only the rate is nullified and deemed not written into the contract; the parties' agreement on the payment of interest remains," and the legal rate prevailing at the time of the agreement applies.
suggestedAnswer.application: L bears the burden of justifying 36%. Without proof of market conditions and equal bargaining positions, the court may strike the rate and apply the legal rate in effect in 2025.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The rate is suspect; if unjustified, it is replaced by the legal rate, but interest remains due. **Bar trap:** striking down an unconscionable rate does not erase the obligation to pay interest.

keyPoints: Lifting of usury ceilings is not a carte blanche for lenders
Unconscionability depends on the context of each case
Legal rate = presumptive reasonable compensation; more than twice the legal rate is suspect
Creditor must prove market conditions and equal footing
Only the rate is nullified; the legal rate at the time of the agreement applies

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part II(B) (unconscionability of stipulated interest)
source.excerpt: The legal rate of interest is the presumptive reasonable compensation for borrowed money. While parties are free to deviate from this, any deviation must be reasonable and fair. Any deviation that is far-removed is suspect. Thus, in cases where stipulated interest is more than twice the prevailing legal rate of interest, it is for the creditor to prove that this rate is required by prevailing market conditions. (Emphasis supplied) Conformable to the foregoing pronouncements, "[t]he maximum interest rate that will not cross the line of conscionability is 'not more than twice the prevailing legal rate of interest.' If the stipulated interest exceeds this standard, the creditor must show that the rate is necessary under current market conditions." The creditor must also show that the parties were on an equal footing when they stipulated on the interest rate. Furthermore, where the monetary interest rate is found to be unconscionable, only the rate is nullified and deemed not written into the contract; the parties' agreement on the payment of interest remains. In such instance, "the legal rate of interest prevailing at the time the agreement was entered into" is applied by the courts.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A seller sold goods on a 60-day credit term, with 24% interest a year on overdue accounts. The trial court awarded the seller the price plus 24% interest from judicial demand. Only the buyer appealed. On appeal, the Supreme Court added legal interest on the accrued 24% interest under Article 2212. On reconsideration, how did the Court characterize the transaction and the 24% interest, and what did it do with the added award? Explain, citing the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court held that the contract was not a loan or forbearance of money, goods or credit but a sale of goods on credit, and that the 24% was compensatory interest imposed as indemnity for the delay in paying the price under Article 2209. Although Article 2212 could in principle apply to that accrued interest, the added award was deleted because the seller did not appeal, so granting it on the buyer's appeal was ultra vires.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2022 Resolution, the Court modified its 2019 Decision and held "that the contract involved is not a loan or forbearance of money, goods, or credit, but a sale of goods on credit." The 24% would run only upon the buyer's failure to pay on the due date, so it was a compensatory interest under Article 2209, and by Article 2212 the accrued compensatory interest may earn interest on interest. However, the trial court's award "became final and executory as to Midtown Industrial Sales as it did not appeal. Thus, the additional award of legal interest on the 24% interest, in an appeal brought by Lara's Gifts, is ultra vires." The Court also noted that the unconscionability standards cannot apply to interest on interest under Article 2212, which is fixed by law.
suggestedAnswer.application: The buyer still pays the principal with 24% interest from the extrajudicial demand until full payment, and the attorney's fees, but not the legal interest on the 24% interest.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Sale on credit; 24% compensatory; the extra award deleted. **Bar trap:** an appellee who did not appeal cannot obtain affirmative relief beyond what the judgment gave it.

keyPoints: Sale of goods on credit, not a loan or forbearance
The 24% ran only upon default: compensatory interest under Art. 2209
Art. 2212 interest on interest could apply, and it is fixed by law (no unconscionability test)
The seller did not appeal: the judgment was final as to it
Adding relief on the buyer's appeal was ultra vires; the award was deleted

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part III (application to the case)
source.excerpt: Now to this case, we modify our earlier Decision and hold that the contract involved is not a loan or forbearance of money, goods, or credit, but a sale of goods on credit. From January to December 2007, petitioner Lara's Gifts purchased from respondent Midtown various industrial and construction materials totaling ₱1,263,104.22. The purchases were on a 60-day credit term, with the condition that a 24% interest rate per annum would be charged on all accounts overdue. This means that the 24% interest rate per annum would run only upon petitioner's failure to pay on the due date. Thus, the 24% interest rate is a compensatory interest, imposed as indemnity for damages caused by the delay in the payment of the raw materials' purchase price, pursuant to Article 2209. By the express provision of Article 2212, the 24% compensatory interest, which have accrued at the time of judicial demand, may be subject to "interest on interest." However, as Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier pointed out, the Regional Trial Court adjudged in favor of Midtown Industrial Sales only P1,263,104.22 plus interest at 24% per annum, computed from February 5, 2008 until fully paid; and P50,000.00 as attorney's fees. This judgment award became final and executory as to Midtown Industrial Sales as it did not appeal. Thus, the additional award of legal interest on the 24% interest, in an appeal brought by Lara's Gifts, is ultra vires.

Its imposition is not subject to the court's discretionary power." **B, C and D are wrong:** none is the reason given. **Bar trap:** Article 2212 is deemed written into every contract with stipulated interest.

questions.prompt: X Corp., an exporter, sues its bank for moral damages after the bank's error caused several of X Corp.'s checks to bounce, leading suppliers to cancel its credit line and hold its orders. The bank argues that a corporation, not being a natural person, can never recover moral damages. Is the bank correct? Explain, citing Simex International v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Not entirely. As a rule a corporation is not entitled to moral damages, but there is an exception where the corporation has a good reputation that is debased, resulting in its social humiliation; X Corp. falls within it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Simex v. CA, the Court held that "a corporation is not as a rule entitled to moral damages because, not being a natural person, it cannot experience physical suffering or such sentiments as wounded feelings, serious anxiety, mental anguish and moral shock. The only exception to this rule is where the corporation has a good reputation that is debased, resulting in its social humiliation." The bouncing checks impaired the corporation's prestige and diminished confidence in it as a reliable debtor.
suggestedAnswer.application: X Corp.'s credit line was canceled and its orders were held because its checks bounced, so its good name in the business community was damaged by the bank's fault. One past collection suit does not show it had no good reputation to protect.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: X Corp. may recover moral damages under the exception. **Bar trap:** the rule (no moral damages for corporations) has an exception for a debased good reputation; know both.

keyPoints: General rule: a corporation cannot recover moral damages (it cannot feel suffering or anguish)
Exception: its good reputation is debased, resulting in social humiliation
Bouncing checks impaired its prestige and its standing as a reliable debtor
Credit line canceled, orders held, business declined
A single past collection case did not show it had no good name

The only exception to this rule is where the corporation has a good reputation that is debased, resulting in its social humiliation. We shall recognize that the petitioner did suffer injury because of the private respondent's negligence that caused the dishonor of the checks issued by it. The immediate consequence was that its prestige was impaired because of the bouncing checks and confidence in it as a reliable debtor was diminished.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The trial court found that a bank negligently failed to credit a depositor's deposit, causing its checks to bounce and its business to suffer. Since the depositor could not prove the exact peso amount of its losses, the court awarded only ₱20,000 as nominal damages. Was the award proper? Explain the purpose of moral damages and of nominal damages, citing Simex International v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Since the depositor proved it suffered loss, the proper award is moral damages, not nominal damages; the lack of proof of the exact amount does not bar moral damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Simex v. CA, the Court held that moral damages "are not awarded to penalize the defendant but to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries he may have suffered." Their amount need not be established with exactitude, because "[m]oral damages are not susceptible of pecuniary estimation"; Article 2216 provides that no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary for moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages, and the amount is left to the court's discretion. Under Article 2221, nominal damages are adjudicated to vindicate or recognize a violated right, "and not for the purpose of indemnifying the plaintiff for any loss suffered by him."
suggestedAnswer.application: Because the depositor proved a real loss (canceled credit line, held orders, declined business, tarnished reputation), nominal damages were the wrong remedy. In the case, the Court replaced the ₱20,000 nominal damages with ₱20,000 moral damages, and added ₱50,000 exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Moral damages, not nominal damages, should be awarded. **Bar trap:** nominal damages are for a violated right without proven loss; once a loss is shown, they are not the proper relief.

keyPoints: Moral damages compensate, they do not penalize
Not susceptible of pecuniary estimation; no proof of pecuniary loss needed (Art. 2216)
Amount left to the court's discretion
Nominal damages (Art. 2221): vindicate a right, not indemnify a loss
Loss proved: moral damages in lieu of nominal damages

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (purpose and proof) and nominal damages
source.excerpt: We agree that moral damages are not awarded to penalize the defendant but to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries he may have suffered. In the case at bar, the petitioner is seeking such damages for the prejudice sustained by it as a result of the private respondent's fault. The respondent court said that the claimed losses are purely speculative and are not supported by substantial evidence, but if failed to consider that the amount of such losses need not be established with exactitude precisely because of their nature. Moral damages are not susceptible of pecuniary estimation. Article 2216 of the Civil Code specifically provides that "no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary in order that moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages may be adjudicated." … Under Article 2221 of the Civil Code, "nominal damages are adjudicated in order that a right of the plaintiff, which has been violated or invaded by the defendant, may be vindicated or recognized, and not for the purpose of indemnifying the plaintiff for any loss suffered by him." As we have found that the petitioner has indeed incurred loss through the fault of the private respondent, the proper remedy is the award to it of moral damages, which we impose, in our discretion, in the same amount of P20,000.00.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bank failed to credit a deposit, causing a depositor's checks to bounce. When told of the error, it took a week to correct it and never explained why it happened. The bank argues that exemplary damages are improper because it eventually corrected its records and the checks were paid. Rule on the bank's argument, citing Simex International v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The argument fails. Given a bank's fiduciary duty to treat its depositors' accounts with meticulous care, its unexplained error and its delay in correcting it were wanton, warranting exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Simex v. CA, the Court held that, "as a business affected with public interest and because of the nature of its functions, the bank is under obligation to treat the accounts of its depositors with meticulous care, always having in mind the fiduciary nature of their relationship." Having been informed of its error, the bank corrected it only a week later, 23 days after the deposit, with no satisfactory explanation; "[s]uch ineptness comes under the concept of the wanton manner contemplated in the Civil Code that calls for the imposition of exemplary damages" (Art. 2232).
suggestedAnswer.application: Correcting the error late does not excuse it: the error should not have been made at all, and the checks should have been paid on presentment. The bank's lackadaisical attitude was gross negligence. The Court imposed ₱50,000 exemplary damages as a deterrent.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Exemplary damages are proper. **Bar trap:** a later correction does not erase a bank's breach of its high duty of care; the standard for banks is meticulous care, given the fiduciary nature of the relationship.

keyPoints: Banks are businesses affected with public interest
Duty to treat depositors' accounts with meticulous care; fiduciary relationship
Unexplained error and a week's delay in correcting it after notice
Such ineptness is "wanton" under Art. 2232: exemplary damages
₱50,000 exemplary damages as a warning and deterrent

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of exemplary damages (duty of banks)
source.excerpt: The point is that as a business affected with public interest and because of the nature of its functions, the bank is under obligation to treat the accounts of its depositors with meticulous care, always having in mind the fiduciary nature of their relationship. In the case at bar, it is obvious that the respondent bank was remiss in that duty and violated that relationship. What is especially deplorable is that, having been informed of its error in not crediting the deposit in question to the petitioner, the respondent bank did not immediately correct it but did so only one week later or twenty-three days after the deposit was made. It bears repeating that the record does not contain any satisfactory explanation of why the error was made in the first place and why it was not corrected immediately after its discovery. Such ineptness comes under the concept of the wanton manner contemplated in the Civil Code that calls for the imposition of exemplary damages.

Its business certainly is not that big, or its name that prestigious," and it imposed moral damages of ₱20,000 in lieu of nominal damages. **A is wrong:** the amount is still left to the court's sound discretion. **C is wrong:** the exception for a debased reputation applied. **D is wrong:** the Court fixed the amount itself. **Bar trap:** discretion over the amount means the court may grant much less than claimed.

choices.B: The judgment for ₱20,000 nominal damages was affirmed.
